hook: Ten people. Ten places. Ten claims that the same thing happened to them, and that hours of their lives are missing.
narration:
Ten people. Ten places. Ten claims that the same thing happened to them, and that hours of their lives are missing.

This is not a list of UFO sightings. It is not a list of strange lights in the sky. It is a list of the ten times someone said they were taken — into a craft they could not identify, by beings they could not describe, and returned hours later, sometimes days later, with no memory of where they had been and no way to prove they had ever left.

You will hear about a Brazilian farmer who claimed something happened to him in nineteen fifty-seven. A police officer in Nebraska who pulled over, in the middle of his shift, for what he thought was a stalled truck. A logger in Arizona who disappeared in front of his entire crew and came back five days later. Two camp counselors in Vermont who, a decade after their summer job, separately described the same craft to the same investigator, in the same words, neither knowing what the other was saying.

Some of these cases have been investigated by the United States Air Force. Some were the subject of formal medical examinations. Some have been openly classified as hoaxes. Some have never been classified at all.

We are not going to tell you what to believe. We are going to tell you what each of these people said happened, what investigators found when they checked, and what is still unexplained.

We are going to count down from ten to one.

Before we begin, if these cases are why you came here, subscribe to the channel. We tell one of these every week, sourced from primary records. That subscribe button is the only reason we can keep going.

Number ten. The Schirmer abduction. Ashland, Nebraska. December the third, nineteen sixty-seven.

It is two-thirty in the morning. Sergeant Herbert Schirmer of the Ashland police department is patrolling Highway Sixty-Three, the same patrol he has driven hundreds of times. He is twenty-two years old. He is two months into the job.

He sees what he first thinks is a stalled truck. Red lights, low to the ground, off the shoulder of the road. He pulls his cruiser closer. The truck is not a truck. It is a metallic, oval-shaped object hovering a few feet above the highway. As Schirmer's headlights catch it, the object rises silently and disappears into the sky.

Schirmer drives back to the station. He logs the sighting. He notices a red welt on the side of his neck, and he cannot remember what happened in the twenty minutes between leaving the highway and arriving back at the station. Twenty minutes during which his patrol log shows no radio activity at all.

The case is taken up by the Condon Committee, the University of Colorado UFO study commissioned by the United States Air Force. They send Schirmer to a psychologist named Leo Sprinkle for hypnotic regression. Under hypnosis, Schirmer says that the occupants of the craft brought him aboard. They were small. They communicated with him without speaking. They told him that they would visit him twice more in his lifetime, and that some day he would, in his words, see the universe.

The Condon Committee's official conclusion is that something happened to Herbert Schirmer that night, but they cannot say what. The recovered memories are dismissed as unreliable. The unaccounted twenty minutes are not.

Schirmer left the police force in nineteen sixty-eight. He told the same story for the rest of his life.

But Schirmer was alone. The next case, just six months later, had two witnesses. And ten years after the abduction, both of them, separately, described the same room.

Number nine. The Buff Ledge Camp abduction. Lake Champlain, Vermont. August the seventh, nineteen sixty-eight.

Buff Ledge is a private girls' summer camp on the western shore of Lake Champlain. On the afternoon of August seventh, the camp's two part-time staff are sitting on the boat dock during their break. Michael Lapp is sixteen years old. Janet Cornell is nineteen. She is the water-ski instructor.

It is just after sunset. They see a bright light in the western sky, low and slow. Other staff at the camp see it too. But for Lapp and Cornell on the dock, the light comes closer. They later say they remember the craft, then they remember being on the boat dock again. The light is gone. Their watches are not synchronised. Neither speaks about the experience that summer. They go back to work.

Ten years later, in nineteen seventy-eight, Lapp writes a letter to the astronomer Walter Webb, who works for the Center for UFO Studies in Chicago. Lapp tells Webb that he has had recurring nightmares about the night on the dock and that he believes something happened to him that he cannot remember.

Webb interviews Lapp. He tracks down Janet Cornell, now a working adult elsewhere on the East Coast. He arranges hypnotic regression for both. Critically, he conducts the sessions separately. Lapp does not know what Cornell says. Cornell does not know what Lapp says.

The two accounts are nearly identical. The same craft. The same beings. The same medical examination room. The same small-detail descriptions of the surfaces of the walls. Webb spends five years checking for collusion. He cannot find any.

In nineteen ninety-four, Webb publishes a three-hundred-page monograph on the case. He concludes that the two witnesses are telling him what they remember.

But Buff Ledge had two witnesses. The next case had four men. And one of them, decades later, said the entire thing was made up.

Number eight. The Allagash Abductions. Allagash Wilderness, Maine. August the twentieth, nineteen seventy-six.

In August nineteen seventy-six, four men in their twenties take a two-week canoeing trip into the Allagash Waterway in northern Maine. Twin brothers Jack and Jim Weiner. Their friends Chuck Rak and Charles Foltz. They are art students from the Massachusetts College of Art.

On the night of August twentieth, they are fishing from a canoe near Eagle Lake. They have built a large fire on the shore so they can find their way back. They see what they describe as a large, glowing sphere over the lake. They paddle for shore. They reach the shore. They look back. The sphere is gone. The fire they had built, which should have burned for another hour, is reduced to smoldering coals.

For more than a decade afterwards, all four men have recurring nightmares. They each, independently, describe being floated up into the sphere. They each describe being in a room. They each describe a medical examination.

In nineteen eighty-eight, they contact the UFO investigator Raymond Fowler. Fowler arranges hypnotic regression sessions, conducted separately, with a doctor named Anthony Constantino. The four accounts, again, are consistent.

Fowler publishes a book, The Allagash Abductions, in nineteen ninety-three. The case becomes one of the most cited multi-witness abduction reports in UFO literature.

Then, in twenty-sixteen, Chuck Rak gives an interview. He says the abduction story was not real. He says he had seen lights over the lake during the trip, but the rest had been embellished, in his words, for financial gain.

The other three men dispute Rak's retraction. They say what they remembered under hypnosis is what happened.

The case is now exactly as divided as the witnesses are. Three say it happened. One says it didn't. There is no way to tell which one is lying, or whether all four are.

But Allagash divides on memory. The next case had two witnesses, and a tape recorder running while they thought they were alone.

Number seven. The Pascagoula incident. Pascagoula, Mississippi. October the eleventh, nineteen seventy-three.

It is just after seven in the evening. Forty-two-year-old shipyard worker Charles Hickson and his nineteen-year-old co-worker Calvin Parker are fishing from a pier on the west bank of the Pascagoula River. The Singing River, the locals call it.

Hickson hears a whirring sound behind them. Parker turns around. A blue-grey object, oval, about thirty feet long, is hovering a few feet above the river bank. From it emerge three figures. Hickson later describes them as having grey, wrinkled skin, slits where eyes and a nose should be, and pincers where hands should be.

Parker faints. Hickson is conscious for what follows. He says the figures float him into the craft. He is examined. He is then placed back on the river bank. The craft is gone.

Hickson and Parker drive to the local Air Force base, then to the Jackson County Sheriff's office. They tell the deputies what happened. The deputies, who have heard a great many strange stories and are sceptical of this one, leave the two men alone in an interview room. They have left a tape recorder running, hoping to catch the men saying that the story is fabricated.

The recording is later transcribed. The two men, alone in the room, do not laugh. They do not change the story. Hickson, on the tape, says he is afraid no one will believe them, and that they should leave town. Parker, on the tape, can be heard crying.

The deputies played the tape for sceptics for the rest of their careers. They said that whatever Hickson and Parker thought had happened, they were not lying about it.

In twenty-nineteen, the city of Pascagoula installed a historical marker at the site. Calvin Parker died in twenty-twenty-three, age sixty-eight, telling the same story he told when he was nineteen.

But Pascagoula had two witnesses, and only the witnesses claimed contact. The next case had eleven witnesses, and they fired a shotgun at what was approaching their farmhouse for nearly four hours.

Number six. The Kelly-Hopkinsville encounter. Christian County, Kentucky. The night of August the twenty-first, nineteen fifty-five.

Eleven members of the Sutton family are at the family farmhouse near the village of Kelly. Five adults. Six children. They have a visiting house guest, a Pennsylvania man named Billy Ray Taylor.

At seven in the evening, Taylor walks out to the well to fetch water. He sees, in his words, a metallic object trailing fire come down into a gully near the farmhouse. He runs back to tell the others. The others laugh.

An hour later, the family dog starts barking. Elmer Sutton goes to the back door and opens it. Standing on the back step is a small figure, three to four feet tall, with oversized hands and large, glowing yellow eyes. Sutton fires his shotgun at it.

For the next four hours, the family inside the farmhouse fire shotguns and twenty-two-caliber rifles at small figures that appear at every window. They report that the figures float, that bullets seem to bounce off them, and that they always appear silently and at multiple windows simultaneously.

At eleven in the evening, the family piles into two cars and drives to Hopkinsville. They go to the Hopkinsville police station. The desk sergeant, looking at five terrified adults and seven crying children, dispatches every officer in the county to the farmhouse.

The police find no figures. They find shotgun shells. They find bullet holes through the screens. They find the family, when they return with them, refusing to go inside.

By morning the figures are gone. The Air Force investigates and classifies the case, in their Project Blue Book file, as a hoax involving great horned owls. UFO researchers have spent seventy years pointing out that the Suttons were experienced rural shooters and that bullet holes through screens are not consistent with owl observation.

The Suttons never recanted. None of the eleven witnesses ever broke from the original account.

We are halfway through. Five cases to go. So far we have heard a police officer, two camp counselors, four campers in Maine, two fishermen on a Mississippi pier, and a family of eleven in rural Kentucky. The cases ahead are the ones the men who did the investigating considered the most consequential.

Number five. The Manhattan Abduction. New York City. November the thirtieth, nineteen eighty-nine.

Linda Napolitano is a thirty-eight-year-old housewife living on the twelfth floor of an apartment building on the Lower East Side. She is in contact with the UFO researcher Budd Hopkins, having earlier reported recurring strange dreams.

In November nineteen eighty-nine, Napolitano contacts Hopkins to tell him that she believes she has been taken. She describes being floated out of her bedroom window by a beam of blue light. The bedroom window is on the twelfth floor, three hundred and fifty feet above the East River.

Hopkins, having heard versions of this story before, takes notes and waits.

In nineteen ninety-one, Hopkins receives a letter. It is from two men who say they were security officers, parked under the F D R Drive on the night of November thirtieth, nineteen eighty-nine. The letter says that the men, in their car, looked up and saw a woman in a white nightgown, accompanied by three small figures, floating up out of the side of an apartment building, into a hovering craft, which then dove into the East River.

A third witness, a woman crossing the Brooklyn Bridge at the same hour, contacts Hopkins independently and describes the same scene.

The two security officers, in subsequent investigation, claim they were escorting a senior diplomat in the back of their car at the time. They claim that the diplomat was Javier Pérez de Cuéllar, then Secretary-General of the United Nations.

Hopkins publishes the case in his nineteen ninety-six book, Witnessed.

The Secretary-General has, on multiple occasions, denied any abduction experience. The two security officers have never been independently identified. The third witness has never been independently identified.

The case has been called the most witnessed alien abduction in history, and the case has been called an entirely fabricated piece of UFO folklore. There is no evidence that has settled it either way.

Linda Napolitano sued the streaming service Netflix in twenty-twenty-four over its docuseries portrayal of the case. She is, as of this recording, alive and continuing to defend her account.

But Linda Cortile claimed contact with multiple witnesses. The next case sold two million copies of a book about it.

Number four. The Whitley Strieber experience. Upstate New York. December the twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-five.

Whitley Strieber is a forty-year-old novelist with a successful career writing horror fiction. The Wolfen. The Hunger. He is married. He has a young son. He owns a cabin in the Catskill Mountains, where the family spends weekends.

On the night of December the twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-five, the family goes to bed at the cabin around ten in the evening. Strieber later says he wakes up to find himself in a circular room, surrounded by figures. Then nothing. Then he is back in bed.

He does not, at first, remember what he experienced. The memory comes back to him in fragments over the next two weeks. He becomes anxious. He cannot work. He goes to a therapist. The therapist refers him to Budd Hopkins.

Hopkins arranges hypnotic regression. Strieber, under hypnosis, describes the figures in detail. Small. Grey. Oversized black almond-shaped eyes. Strieber, who is a professional writer, sketches what he remembers. The drawing becomes the cover of his book.

In nineteen eighty-seven, he publishes Communion. The book sells more than two million copies. The cover image, which Strieber drew, becomes the single most recognisable depiction of an alien being in popular culture. Almost every grey alien you have ever seen in a film, on a t-shirt, in a meme, traces back to that drawing.

Strieber refuses to call the figures aliens. He calls them visitors. He says he does not know what they were. He says they may have been human. He says they may have been from somewhere else. He has spent the rest of his life trying to find out, in a series of follow-up books, none of which have ever sold the way Communion did.

He is alive. He still tells the same story. He still refuses to claim certainty.

But Strieber's case was a writer in a cabin alone. The next case, decades earlier, was a Brazilian farmer alone in a field, and the doctor who examined him afterwards found something he could not explain.

Number three. The Antônio Villas Boas case. Minas Gerais, Brazil. October the fifteenth, nineteen fifty-seven.

Antônio Villas Boas is a twenty-three-year-old farmer working his family's land in the south of Brazil. He plows at night to avoid the heat of the day. On the night of October fifteenth, nineteen fifty-seven, he is plowing alone by tractor when a red light descends from the sky and the tractor's engine cuts out.

He is, by his account, taken out of the tractor by four men in tight grey suits and helmets. He is taken into the craft. He is examined. The four figures take blood from his chin. They wipe his body with a clear gel.

He is then released back to his field. He estimates four hours have passed.

By morning, Villas Boas is suffering from nausea, headaches, vomiting, and lesions on his skin that look like radiation burns.

The case becomes public when his mother contacts a journalist named José Martins. Martins refers him to a doctor named Olavo Fontes, a professor of medicine at the National School of Medicine in Rio de Janeiro. Fontes examines Villas Boas in February nineteen fifty-eight, four months after the alleged event.

Fontes's medical report is the part of this case that, sixty-eight years later, has not been explained. Fontes documents skin lesions consistent with exposure to ionising radiation. He notes that the patient's blood count shows damage of the kind associated with radiation poisoning. He notes scars on the chin matching where Villas Boas had said the blood was drawn. Fontes is not a UFO researcher. He is a doctor.

Antônio Villas Boas later becomes a lawyer. He marries. He raises four children. He never speaks publicly about the case. He gives a single interview, at the end of his life, in nineteen ninety. He died in nineteen ninety-one. He never altered any detail.

His case was the first detailed alien-abduction account in modern history. The cases that came after it inherited every element of his story.

But Villas Boas was a single witness. The next case had six.

Number two. The Travis Walton incident. Snowflake, Arizona. November the fifth, nineteen seventy-five.

Travis Walton is a twenty-two-year-old logger working on a Forest Service contract with a six-man crew. They are clearing brush in the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest. At the end of the day, around six in the evening, they pile into a truck to drive home.

About halfway down a forest road, they see a glowing disc-shaped craft hovering above a clearing. The crew chief stops the truck. Walton, against the warnings of the others, gets out and walks toward the object.

The other six men later say that as Walton approached, a beam of light shot down from the craft, struck him, and threw him backwards onto the ground. They panic. The driver speeds away.

When they return fifteen minutes later, Walton is gone. The craft is gone.

The crew goes to the Navajo County Sheriff. They tell their story. The sheriff considers them suspects in a possible homicide. Walton's brothers, who do not know whether he is alive or dead, demand a search. Five hundred volunteers comb the forest for five days.

On the morning of November the eleventh, Walton calls his sister's house from a payphone in Heber, Arizona, twelve miles from where he had vanished. He is dehydrated, has lost ten pounds, and is wearing the same clothes he had been wearing five days earlier.

Walton says he was taken aboard the craft. He says he was examined by figures who looked like nothing he had seen before. He says he does not know how he got back.

The Sheriff's department insists on polygraph tests. The six crew members are tested. Five pass clearly. One result is inconclusive. The polygraph examiner, who has worked for the Arizona Department of Public Safety for twenty years, states on the record that he believes the men are telling the truth.

Walton himself takes a polygraph in nineteen ninety-three, administered by a former examiner from the Central Intelligence Agency. He passes. He has taken at least four polygraphs in his life. He has never failed.

Travis Walton, as of this recording, is seventy-two years old. He has told the same story for fifty years.

But Walton was found four days after he disappeared. The next case lost two hours, and started everything that came after.

Number one. The Betty and Barney Hill abduction. New Hampshire. The night of September the nineteenth, nineteen sixty-one.

Betty and Barney Hill are a couple in their forties. Betty is a social worker. Barney is a postal worker. They are driving home from a vacation in Niagara Falls and Montreal, on US Route Three, in northern New Hampshire, when they see a bright object low in the sky.

Barney pulls over. He gets out of the car with a pair of binoculars. Through the binoculars, he later says, he can see figures looking back at him through the windows of the craft. He becomes convinced they intend to capture him. He runs back to the car. He and Betty drive south.

They arrive home at five in the morning. They expect to have been driving for around two hours less than they have been. They cannot account for the missing time.

Betty's dress, packed in the suitcase since the trip, is, when she opens it days later, torn and stained with a pink substance that no one ever identifies. Barney's shoe is scuffed in a way it was not at the start of the trip. The binoculars' strap is broken.

For three years, both of them have nightmares. Betty dreams in detail about a craft and figures. She begins writing the dreams down. Barney does not speak about his.

In January nineteen sixty-four, the Hills consult a Boston psychiatrist named Benjamin Simon. Simon conducts hypnotic regression sessions, separately, with each of them. He is sceptical. He suspects he is dealing with a shared delusion.

Under hypnosis, the two of them, separately, describe the same craft. The same figures. The same examination room. The same conversation. Betty describes a star map shown to her by one of the figures. Years later, an Ohio schoolteacher named Marjorie Fish constructs a three-dimensional model of the stars within fifty light-years of Earth and matches Betty's hand-drawn map to a specific binary star system, Zeta Reticuli, which had not been catalogued in nineteen sixty-one.

The case is investigated by the United States Air Force as part of Project Blue Book. It is classified as unknown.

Every alien-abduction story you have ever heard inherits something from the Hills. The missing time. The hypnotic regression. The grey beings. The star map. The Hills are the founding case. They are the case the others answer to.

Betty Hill died in two thousand four. Barney Hill died in nineteen sixty-nine. Neither of them changed any part of their account.

Ten cases. Ten people. Ten claims that something happened to them that they could not explain, that did not stop happening to them, and that they did not, when given every opportunity, retract.

A police officer in Nebraska. A girls' camp in Vermont. Four campers in Maine. Two fishermen on a Mississippi river. Eleven members of one family in Kentucky. A housewife in Manhattan. A novelist in the Catskills. A farmer in Brazil. A logger in Arizona. A couple driving home through New Hampshire.

Some of these cases have been investigated by the United States Air Force. Some by university committees. Some by independent investigators with decades of training. None of the investigators, on any of these ten cases, was ever able to prove the witnesses were lying.

That is not the same thing as proving the witnesses were right.

If you watched all the way to the end, you are the reason this channel exists. Like the video. If you want more cases like these, subscribe. We tell one of these every week, sourced from primary records, and we do not tell you what to believe. We tell you what was reported and what investigators found.

Next week, ten unsolved disappearances on commercial flights. The kind of case where the plane was found and no one was on it.

Until then. Thank you for watching.
